name: Morning height measurement trick

lead: People are slightly taller in the morning than in the evening, so measuring just after getting out of bed gives your highest figure of the day. Forum users use it to report a higher number and to track height-related changes on a consistent basis.

Spinal discs compress during upright activity and recover when lying down, so stature falls over the day and returns overnight. One study cited by Wikipedia found children's heights dropped by a mean of about 1.5 cm between waking and mid-afternoon, and clinical practice uses a stadiometer with standardised posture as the reference method.

paras: People measure shortly after waking, barefoot against a wall or stadiometer, at the same time each day so readings can be compared. Posture, shoes and measurement technique add further variation, and some forum posters also discuss supplements, core strength and insoles for keeping morning height through the day, though no studies were found supporting those.

There are no meaningful health risks in measuring. The main caveat is measurement error: a typical error of about half a centimetre can hide small real changes, and self-reported heights tend to differ from measured values.

chain: Spine is least compressed after waking
angle.text: Measuring shortly after waking, when the spine is least compressed, records your daily maximum height, a figure about a centimetre or more above the evening reading. It also gives a consistent baseline for tracking height changes.

lead: The morning height measurement trick is the practice of measuring height shortly after waking, when stature is at its daily maximum, instead of later in the day. People use it to record the largest figure of the day, to track height-related changes under the same conditions each time, and to settle what their "real" height is. It is discussed on height and looksmaxxing forums, where posters compare night and morning readings and trade ways to keep morning height for longer.

The effect behind it is documented. Wikipedia reports that height changes over the day, that lying down for long periods raises it and that vigorous exercise before measuring lowers it, and cites a study of 100 children whose heights fell by a mean of 1.54 cm between getting out of bed and mid-afternoon.[1] Adult research on spinal shrinkage found a circadian height variation averaging 14.4 mm in one 1986 sports-science study, and recent radiotherapy imaging studies measured the spine shortening by under a millimetre per hour in adults and about 1 mm over a day in children.[2][3][4]

Clinical practice measures height with a stadiometer, a vertical ruler with a sliding headpiece, with the subject barefoot and standing erect against it.[5] Forum posters also discuss ways to keep morning height through the day, including supplements, core strength and insoles; no studies of those methods were found.

sections.h: Why height varies over the day
paras: Stature is not constant across the day. Wikipedia reports that lying down for a long period raises measured height, and that exercise immediately before measuring lowers it; the same article cites a study of 100 children who were on average about 1.54 cm shorter between 4 and 5 p.m. than on waking.[1]

The spine contains 23 intervertebral discs, and the nucleus of each disc holds water drawn in by negatively charged proteoglycans; under compressive load the disc distributes pressure outward, and over a lifetime loss of disc water and size contributes to the common decrease of height with age.[6] Many height guides attribute the daily swing to the same disc behaviour, with discs compressing under upright activity and re-expanding while lying down.

Height loss over decades is a related but separate phenomenon: shrinking can begin in middle age in some people and is nearly universal in the very old, with drying discs, soft-tissue wasting and posture changes among the causes, and excessive loss can signal osteoporosis.[1][7]

Standing height is measured with a stadiometer in children over two and adults who can stand unaided; shorter or less mobile subjects are measured lying down or estimated with surrogates such as knee height, arm span or ulna length [1][8]. Wikipedia notes that measurement error is a limitation, and that a typical error of 0.5 cm can make small real growth look like negative growth or more than it is [1].

Grokipedia describes the reference measurement protocol as barefoot with heels, buttocks, shoulders and head against the backboard, and states that tape measures can add variability from sagging or inconsistent application [5]. A study of vertebral fractures reports that serial height measurement is used to monitor height loss in older adults [7].

Wikipedia gives a typical measurement error of about 0.5 cm and notes that infants under two are measured lying down, with recumbent length about 0.7 cm more than standing height.[1] The same article states that self-reported heights tend to be higher than measured heights, with the gap varying by height, age, sex and region.[1]

Researchers call the daily loss of stature spinal shrinkage and have used it as a measure of how much load the spine carries. A 1986 study in the British Journal of Sports Medicine used standing-height loss to compare spinal loading in circuit weight training (10 men), a 6 km run by novice runners (9 men) and a 25 km run by trained runners (7 men). Height loss was about 5.4 mm after weight training and about 3.25 mm after the novices' run, and experienced runners lost roughly 0.4 mm per kilometre. Circadian height variation in the same study averaged 14.4 mm, which exceeded the change during the 25 km run, and height was regained overnight during sleep but not during a 20-minute rest after exercise.[2]

Radiotherapy planning has produced recent imaging measurements. A 2025 study of 13 craniospinal irradiation patients compared daily setup images with the planning CT and found the distance from the base of the skull to the third lumbar vertebra shortened by 0.8 mm per hour, leading the authors to recommend scheduling treatment within two hours of the planning scan.[3] A 2024 retrospective study of 32 paediatric patients (mean age 10) compared morning and afternoon cone-beam CTs and found a median spine-length reduction of 1.0 mm, statistically significant but variable between patients, and not correlated with the time gap between scans of 4 to 9.5 hours.[4]

These measurements use spinal landmarks on imaging rather than a tape-and-wall check, and the whole-body difference reported in the child study is larger than the spinal distances measured on CT, which is one reason posters' own numbers vary.

A National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey analysis examined how age affects the validity of self-reported height, weight and body mass index [9]. Self-reported height is a different matter from the morning-versus-night question, but it is relevant because online discussions of the practice often involve what height a person states.

Practitioners describe the practice in general terms: measure soon after waking, barefoot, standing against a flat wall or stadiometer with heels, buttocks, shoulders and head in contact, which matches the clinical protocol described for stadiometers.[5] Some people measure at both ends of the day and compare, which is how the night-versus-morning figures in forum threads arise.

The convention people choose matters mainly for how a number is reported. Because the daily swing is about a centimetre or more in the cited study, a morning figure and an evening figure can differ by an amount comparable to the measurement error of a casual tape-and-wall check, and clinical guidance emphasises standardised posture and equipment for that reason.[1][5]

A thread titled around night versus morning height has a user reporting about 179.7 cm at night and about 181 cm in the morning and asking whether the average is his real height; replies agree the midpoint would be about 180.35 cm. Another thread lists glucosamine, a stronger core and lower back, and heel insoles as things the poster says help maintain morning height through the day.

No studies found on the morning height measurement trick itself or on glucosamine, core training or insoles for retaining morning height. Related research includes the child study of diurnal height change cited by Wikipedia [1], spinal-shrinkage studies in athletes and radiotherapy patients [2][3][4], measurement work on height loss in older adults [7], and studies of self-reported height [9].

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums, morning versus night height is a recurring question about which figure counts as a person's height.

claims.claim: Morning height is higher than evening height.
Your real height is the average of morning and night.
Glucosamine, core strength and insoles preserve morning height through the day.
Measuring in the morning is how to record your max height.
Staying lying down or hanging before measuring adds height.
Heavy lifting or running before measuring lowers your reading
The difference between morning and night is large enough to change your stated height
